narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 56.1% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors from your academic record. Your class rank at the end of your third year was the strongest influence and pushed the prediction strongly toward failure. Standing in the bottom decile of your class in Year 3 is far below the average performance of students who were accepted, and the model sees this as a clear warning sign for bar exam success. Your first-year class rank was the third most important factor and also pulled the prediction toward failure; again, a bottom-decile placement is much weaker than the typical sixth-decile standing among accepted students.

Your undergraduate GPA worked in the opposite direction. At 3.40 it is higher than the 3.23 average of accepted applicants, so this feature helped push the prediction toward passing. However, its positive effect was not large enough to overcome the negative signals from your class rankings.

Your LSAT score of 29.5 (well below the 37.2 average of accepted students), middle-family income, and plan to attend full-time played smaller roles and did not change the outcome.

To improve your chances, focus on raising your academic performance and retaking the LSAT to demonstrate stronger readiness. Consider reapplying once you have clearer evidence that you can pass the bar on the first try. (218 words)
